title: Negligence suit in shooting death of Toronto boy may proceed, court rules
article: The family of a 15-year-old fatally shot by police in 2006 has passed a major hurdle in a lawsuit against the provincial unit that investigates serious incidents involving police officers.

In a novel 2-1 ruling, Ontario Divisional Court said that the family of Duane Christian may proceed to trial with a $2-million lawsuit that alleges the Special Investigations Unit conducted a negligent, shoddy investigation.
Mr. Christian was killed after two Toronto police constables who had pursued and stopped his van fired several shots to prevent him getting away.

The SIU, an arm\'s-length agency that investigates incidents of serious injury or death involving police officers, was set up by the Ontario government to prevent an appearance of favouritism if police were to investigate members of their own force.

In early 2009, Ontario Ombudsman Andre Marin called the SIU "a toothless tiger and muzzled watchdog" that displays a consistent bias toward police. He was critical of the time it takes SIU investigators to interview police officers and other witnesses after an incident.
The Christian family\'s lawsuit accuses the SIU of failing to question the constable who fired the shots, even though the officer had agreed to be interviewed.
It also faults the SIU for deciding against laying criminal charges without seeing a pathologist\'s report on the incident.

"The SIU\'s investigation was hasty and superficial," said a statement of claim filed on behalf of the Christian family by lawyer Peter Rosenthal. "The SIU rushed to complete the investigation in order to accommodate the officers\' desires to be cleared of any wrongdoing as soon as possible."
The Divisional Court decision is the first ruling to state that investigators may owe a legal duty of care to the victims of an alleged crime.

Writing for the majority, Mr. Justice David McCombs and Madam Justice A. M. Molloy said that recent jurisprudential developments have opened the door to the possibility of victims suing the police for blunders - particularly those made early in an investigation.
"The ability to get information at an early stage can be seen as critically important," they said.
The court rejected an attempt by Ontario\'s Ministry of the Attorney-General to have the lawsuit thrown out for failing to cite a valid cause of action.

Ministry lawyers contended that SIU investigators could become distracted by the potential threat of lawsuits, causing them to feel a "significant chilling effect," and make questionable judgment calls.
"Moreover, it is apparent from the statute that any duties owed by the SIU are owed to the public as a whole, and not to these plaintiffs," the ministry factum said.
A spokesman for the Ministry, Brendan Crawley, said he could not comment on the actual allegations because the case is before the courts.
However, Mr. Rosenthal said in an interview that the decision breaks important ground for victims.
"Allowing this case to go forward opens up possibilities for other victims of negligent investigations," he said.
"The SIU has a responsibility to conduct competent investigations of all killings by police officers. In my view, the investigation was hasty, superficial and grossly incompetent."
Mr. Rosenthal said numerous other questions remained unanswered after the SIU had concluded its investigation. They included:
- why the officers felt they were justified in blocking Mr. Christian\'s van;
- why they felt it was necessary to draw their guns;

- discrepancies between their account of events and the location of spent bullet casings at the scene."The SIU showed disdain for Duane\'s mother and Duane\'s memory with their shoddy investigation," Mr. Rosenthal said.
